analysis.one_liner: Blocks new Gulf of Mexico oil leases for companies that refuse to renegotiate old royalty-free leases.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it was introduced by Rep. Raúl Grijalva with just one cosponsor and died in a House subcommittee after 13 months.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped the Interior Department from issuing any new oil or gas leases in the Gulf of Mexico to companies holding old "royalty relief" leases unless those companies agreed to renegotiate the leases and pay royalties once oil and gas prices crossed certain thresholds. It also would have required Interior, at a company's request, to amend leases issued between 1996 and 2000 in the Central and Western Gulf to add those same price thresholds, effective October 1, 2021. The aim was to end a decades-old arrangement under which some deepwater drillers pump oil from federal waters without paying the royalties other producers owe.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, because royalties from oil taken from federal waters flow to the U.S. Treasury and fund public programs including land and water conservation; the bill also would have pressed legacy leaseholders to pay on the same terms as producers whose leases already carry price thresholds.

how_it_helps.text: Bars Interior from issuing any new Gulf of Mexico oil or gas lease to a company that holds one of the old deepwater royalty-relief leases unless the company first renegotiates that lease to pay royalties once oil and gas prices reach specified thresholds.

Requires Interior to grant, on request, an amendment to any lease issued for a Central or Western Gulf tract between January 1, 1996 and November 28, 2000, adding those price thresholds, with the new terms taking effect October 1, 2021.

Closes the obvious escape hatch: companies could not dodge the requirement by selling, swapping, spinning off, or otherwise transferring a covered lease or its economic benefit to another entity, since any transferee or anyone benefiting from the lease would face the same conditions.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies holding legacy deepwater leases issued under the 1995 Deep Water Royalty Relief Act, which would owe royalties above the price thresholds that they currently do not pay; those costs could also be passed to oil buyers in the form of slightly higher prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gulf of Mexico oil and gas producers

drawbacks.text: The bill would rewrite the financial terms of leases the government deliberately granted as an incentive under the 1995 Deep Water Royalty Relief Act, when deepwater drilling was riskier and more expensive; companies could be expected to challenge forced amendments of signed contracts, and the change could discourage investment in Gulf drilling and reduce future lease-sale bids.

The revenue the bill would recover depends entirely on market prices: royalties would only be owed once oil and gas prices reached the statutory thresholds, so in a low-price environment the bill would collect little or nothing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real but conditional: recovering royalties from a handful of legacy deepwater leaseholders would return public money to the Treasury, but only when prices cross the thresholds, and only from companies that seek new leases or try to acquire covered leases. The cost side is that it reopens contracts the government granted as investment incentives, inviting legal challenges and possibly dampening some offshore investment. On balance it was a modest, targeted fix rather than a broad change, and its main flaw is that it left the recovery entirely to market prices and to companies' own choices about seeking new leases.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Natural Resources Committee and then to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Raúl Grijalva introduced the bill on November 20, 2019, joined by one cosponsor, Rep. Alan Lowenthal; it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
On December 6, 2019, the committee sent it to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, and that was the last action the bill ever received.
The bill sat with no further action for the remaining 13 months of the 116th Congress, which ended January 3, 2021, without a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The oil and gas companies holding legacy deepwater royalty-relief leases came out ahead: because the bill died, they keep producing under leases that require no royalties above the price thresholds, and taxpayers forgo the revenue the bill would have recovered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Legacy Gulf oil leaseholders keep royalty-free production

for.name: Raúl Grijalva
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-AZ); sponsor of the bill and chair of the House Natural Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill; it was referred to the committee he chaired, which never advanced it to the floor.

for.name: Alan Lowenthal
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-CA); the bill's only cosponsor

against.name: Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources
against.role: House Natural Resources subcommittee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the 13 months before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; both the sponsor and the lone cosponsor were Democrats, so the bill never drew a test of where the parties stood.

industries.industry: Gulf of Mexico offshore oil and gas producers
industries.note: Companies holding legacy deepwater leases issued under the 1995 Deep Water Royalty Relief Act would have had to renegotiate those leases to pay royalties above price thresholds, or lose eligibility for new Gulf leases and for acquiring covered leases by sale, swap, or spinoff. Because the bill died, they continue producing without those royalty obligations, and the public keeps covering the revenue that was given up.

industries.industry: Federal Treasury and conservation programs funded by energy royalties
industries.note: Royalties from federal offshore drilling flow to the Treasury and help fund public programs; the bill would have recovered revenue currently forgone on legacy leases, but only when prices crossed the thresholds and only from companies seeking new or transferred leases.
